title: Article 50 Transparency Readiness
description: A step-by-step audit of every AI system that talks to people or generates content, against the transparency obligations in force since 2 August 2026. Work through it once per system, then keep it as evidence.
legal_basis: Article 50 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744; Code of Practice on marking and labelling AI-generated content; Commission guidelines on Article 50 (July 2026)
audience: deployers and providers of chatbots, generative AI, emotion recognition and biometric categorisation

items.text: List every AI system that interacts directly with people: chatbots, voice bots, virtual assistants, automated email or messaging replies.
items.guidance: Include AI features inside SaaS tools you did not build, for example a support-desk bot or a website widget. You are the deployer.

items.text: List every AI system that generates text, images, audio or video, whether for internal use or publication.
items.guidance: Marketing copy generators, image tools, voice cloning, video avatars, summarisers and translation tools all count if the output leaves the organisation.

items.text: List every emotion recognition or biometric categorisation system, and confirm none is used in the workplace or in education.
items.guidance: Workplace and education use is prohibited under Article 5(1)(f) except for medical or safety reasons. Elsewhere it is allowed with disclosure.

items.text: Mark which generative systems were placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2026.
items.guidance: Those systems have until 2 December 2026 to implement machine-readable marking. Systems placed on the market from 2 August 2026 must comply immediately.
items.evidence: Release or go-live date per system

sections.title: 2. Tell people they are dealing with AI (Article 50(1))

items.text: Every chatbot or assistant discloses that it is an AI system at or before the first interaction.
items.guidance: Suggested wording: 'You are chatting with an AI assistant. A human colleague can take over at any time; type "human" to ask.' Do not rely on a line in the terms of service.
items.evidence: Screenshot of the disclosure in the live interface

items.text: Voice and phone systems announce that the caller is speaking with an AI before the conversation starts.
items.guidance: The disclosure must be audible, not only in an IVR menu the caller may skip.

items.text: Hand-off to a human is disclosed when it happens, so people know when the AI stops and a person starts.
items.guidance: Ambiguity about who is talking is the most common complaint the guidelines highlight.

items.text: The disclosure is accessible: readable by screen readers, available in the languages the service is offered in, and not hidden behind a tooltip.
items.guidance: Article 50(5) requires information to be provided in a clear and distinguishable manner, accessible to persons with disabilities.

items.text: For each third-party generative system, the vendor has confirmed in writing how its output is marked (watermark, metadata, content credentials) and how it can be detected.
items.guidance: Ask for the vendor's Article 50(2) statement and whether it has signed the Code of Practice on marking and labelling.

items.text: For generative systems you provide, output is marked in a machine-readable format that is effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible.
items.guidance: Layer techniques: an imperceptible watermark plus provenance metadata such as C2PA content credentials. Document what you chose and why.
items.evidence: Technical note on marking method; sample output with marks verified

items.text: Your editing, compression and publishing pipeline does not strip the marks the model applied.
items.guidance: Test the actual path from generation to publication, including image resizing and social-media upload.

items.text: Legacy generative systems (on the market before 2 August 2026) have a dated plan to be marking output by 2 December 2026.
items.guidance: Owner, milestone dates and a fallback if the vendor will not be ready in time.

items.text: Any published image, audio or video that depicts real people, places or events and is AI-generated or manipulated carries a visible label.
items.guidance: Keep the label on the asset itself, not only in a caption that can be separated from it. Artistic or satirical works may use a lighter label that does not spoil the work.

items.text: AI-generated or manipulated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest is labelled, unless a named person has reviewed it and holds editorial responsibility.
items.guidance: Decide per channel whether you label or apply human editorial review. Record the reviewer for each item you rely on the exemption for.

items.text: A written content policy explains who labels what, in which wording, and the exceptions used.
items.guidance: One page is enough. Link it from the marketing and communications team handbook.

items.text: People exposed to an emotion recognition or biometric categorisation system are informed of its operation before exposure.
items.guidance: Signage, on-screen notice or spoken notice, depending on the setting. Personal data processing must also comply with GDPR.

items.text: One named person owns Article 50 compliance and reviews this checklist at least every six months.
items.guidance: The Commission guidelines and the Code of Practice will keep evolving; assign the regulatory watch.
items.evidence: Owner named in the AI governance policy

items.text: Staff who operate chatbots or produce AI-generated content have completed the Article 50 Readiness Audit module.
items.guidance: This also counts toward Article 4 literacy measures.

items.text: Screenshots, vendor statements, policies and test records for this checklist are stored where they can be produced within days of a request from a market surveillance authority.
items.guidance: Authorities have had enforcement powers since 2 August 2026. Response time matters.

items.text: No system in the inventory generates non-consensual intimate imagery or is capable of being used as a 'nudification' tool.
items.guidance: Prohibited outright since the 2026 amendments. Check image-generation tools for safeguards.

title: Article 4 AI Literacy Evidence Pack
description: The measures and records that show your organisation has taken the AI literacy measures Article 4 requires. Completing the items builds the evidence folder an authority, customer or auditor will ask for.
legal_basis: Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744
audience: every provider and deployer of AI systems

items.text: A short AI literacy policy states that the organisation takes measures to support the AI literacy of staff and others who use AI on its behalf.
items.guidance: Mirror the amended Article 4 wording. One page. Approved by management.
items.evidence: Policy document, version and approval date

items.text: A named owner is responsible for the AI literacy programme and its records.
items.guidance: Often the compliance, HR or IT lead in a small company.

items.text: Roles that operate or rely on AI systems are mapped to the training modules they must complete.
items.guidance: Example: everyone completes the foundation modules; HR adds the HR module; developers add the developer module; marketing adds the customer-facing module.
items.legal_basis: Article 4 (technical knowledge, experience, education, training and context of use)

items.text: Contractors and agency staff who use AI on the organisation's behalf are covered by the same mapping.
items.guidance: Article 4 refers to 'other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf'.

items.text: Completion records exist for every person in scope: module, content version, score, date.
items.guidance: The Article 4 evidence report exports this in one click.

items.text: Certificates are issued for passed modules and stored with the personnel or compliance records.
items.guidance: Not legally required, but the simplest artefact to show a customer or auditor.

items.text: New joiners complete the required modules within their first month.
items.guidance: Add the modules to the onboarding checklist.

items.text: Training is refreshed when the regulation or the tools change, and at least annually.
items.guidance: The 2026 Regulatory Update module exists for exactly this purpose. Record the refresh date.

items.text: Staff have written guidance on acceptable use of AI tools, including what data may be entered and when a human must check the output.
items.guidance: Covers generative AI assistants as well as embedded features in business software.

items.text: Staff know how to report AI behaviour that looks wrong, biased or unsafe, and reports are logged.
items.guidance: A shared inbox or ticket category is enough for a small company.
items.evidence: Escalation route documented; log of reports

items.text: Management reviews the AI literacy programme at least once a year and records the outcome.
items.guidance: Include completion rates, gaps and the plan for the coming year.
